title: Functions and Triggers
subtitle: PL/pgSQL stored functions, trigger functions, and row-level automation
author: KERNAL Team

content.text: The NEW record holds the new row values (for INSERT/UPDATE). OLD holds the previous values (for UPDATE/DELETE). TG_OP is 'INSERT', 'UPDATE', or 'DELETE'. Return NEW from BEFORE triggers to apply changes; return NULL from AFTER triggers (value ignored).

questions.question: You write a BEFORE UPDATE trigger. In the trigger function, you modify NEW.updated_at = NOW() and then RETURN NEW. What happens?
options: The trigger fails — you cannot modify NEW
The update proceeds with the original data, trigger changes are ignored
The update proceeds with the modified row — updated_at is set to NOW()
questions.explanation: In a BEFORE trigger, the returned value is what actually gets written to the table. RETURN NEW applies the (possibly modified) new row. RETURN NULL cancels the operation. So modifying NEW.updated_at = NOW() and returning NEW means the row is saved with the updated timestamp — the calling application does not need to set it explicitly.

faq.q: Should I use triggers or application code?
faq.a: Triggers are good for: (1) updating audit logs, (2) maintaining denormalized data (comment_count), (3) setting updated_at — logic that must happen regardless of how data is modified. Application code is better for complex business logic, sending emails, calling external APIs. Triggers are invisible to the application — both a feature (always runs) and a risk (hard to debug when you don't know they exist).

examples: The set_updated_at() trigger pattern is used in nearly every production PostgreSQL schema — ORMs like Prisma generate it automatically
Supabase uses triggers to fire webhook events when rows change, enabling real-time subscriptions
